# 1 Introduction

## 1.1 Background

Motor insurers need to know whether poor portfolio results come from a broad deterioration or from a small number of identifiable risk segments. A single loss-ratio total is not sufficient because claim frequency, claim severity, exposure duration, policy design, customer loyalty, vehicle profile, and geography can all produce different underwriting implications.

This report uses visual analytics to investigate a Spanish motor insurance portfolio observed from 2022 to 2024. The analysis is framed as a mythbusting exercise: common stereotypes about insurance risk are tested against the data. The objective is not to build a pricing model. The objective is to discover which beliefs are supported by evidence, which are myths, and which are only partially true.

## 1.2 Analytical Objective

The analysis is organised around 10 research questions aligned with three strategic objectives:

1. **Maximise overall portfolio profitability** by identifying segments where loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, or underwriting result point to adverse performance.
2. **Maximise retention and loyalty among low-risk, highly profitable customers** by testing whether longer-observed customers and favourable behavioural signals are associated with better profitability.
3. **Identify high-risk segments for appropriately calibrated premium pricing** by separating stereotypes from evidence-backed signals that can support pricing, excess, coverage, renewal, or monitoring actions.

This makes the data wrangling purposeful: only variables needed to test a myth are retained, recoded, or derived. The guiding visual communication principle is **one-look interpretation**. Static charts, small multiples, and dashboards are preferred over animations because stakeholders should be able to compare segments without relying on memory.

## 1.3 Data Sources

Two source files are used:

- `data/Dataset of motor insurance portfolio.csv`: policy-year motor insurance records.
- `data/Descriptive of variables.xlsx`: variable descriptions and code definitions.

Each row is a policy-year observation. The same insured policy can appear in more than one year.

# 2 Getting Started

# 3 Research Questions and Feature Map

The report uses exactly 10 research questions. Each question starts with an insurance stereotype, then tests whether the stereotype is real, a myth, or mixed. The questions bridge univariate distribution analysis with bivariate profitability analysis by first asking how common each segment is, then asking whether that segment is profitable.

| No. | Myth to test | Research question | Coverage dimension | Useful features | Best-fit visual method |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Young drivers are always the worst risks. | Are younger drivers genuinely less profitable than older drivers? | Conventional and demographic | `driver_age_band`, claims, exposure, loss ratio | Ordered KPI bars and ridgeline distribution |
| 2 | Older vehicles are always riskier. | Does vehicle age increase loss ratio and claim frequency? | Conventional and vehicle factor | `vehicle_age_band`, claims, exposure, loss ratio | Ranked bars and age interaction heatmap |
| 3 | Comprehensive policies are safer because customers pay more. | Which policy types create the most profitability pressure? | Product and coverage design | `policy_type`, premium, incurred, claims | Ranked bars and profitability-status bars |
| 4 | Premium brands are the biggest loss drivers. | Are premium vehicle brands less profitable than mainstream brands? | Brand-and-status | `brand_tier`, claim severity, loss ratio | Point interval and severity comparison |
| 5 | Higher vehicle value always means poorer profitability. | Does vehicle value show a monotonic relationship with loss ratio? | Brand-and-status | `vehicle_value_band`, premium, incurred, claims | Ordered KPI bars |
| 6 | Bad bonus-score customers are always the worst. | Does bonus score separate profitable and unprofitable customers? | Behavioural and claim history proxy | `bonus_score`, loss ratio, claim frequency | Half-eye + boxplot + aggregate point |
| 7 | Short-term policies are harmless because exposure is small. | Are short-exposure policies a hidden profitability problem? | Behavioural and exposure pattern | `exposure_band`, loss ratio, cancellation | Ridgeline density with quantile shading |
| 8 | Loyal customers are just retained volume, not necessarily profitable. | Are longer-observed customers more profitable and worth retaining? | Loyalty and retention | `loyalty_band`, premium, incurred, cancellation | Ranked KPI bars |
| 9 | Cancelled policies are removed risks, so cancellation is good. | Are cancelled policies actually worse risks than active policies? | Loyalty and policy status | `policy_status`, loss ratio, claim frequency | Stacked bars and density comparison |
| 10 | Urban areas are always worse than rural areas. | Does geography materially affect frequency, severity, and loss ratio? | Geographic | `circulation_area`, `municipality_type`, `geo_segment` | Point intervals and geography bars |

The selected methods emphasise practical interpretation. A myth is treated as **real** only when the segment has a visible adverse pattern and a meaningful profitability implication. A myth is **busted** when the common stereotype is contradicted by loss ratio, frequency, severity, or materiality. A myth is **mixed** when the stereotype is true for one risk dimension but not for overall profitability.

## 3.1 Visual Analytics Technique Selection Rationale

The visual analytics methods are selected to serve the three strategic objectives. The report therefore avoids using charts only because they are visually interesting. Each method is chosen because it answers a specific underwriting decision question.

| Strategic objective | Analytical need | Technique selected | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maximise portfolio profitability | Identify which segments are unprofitable and whether the issue is material | `geom_tile()` + `geom_text()` KPI matrices with break-even references where needed | Tile matrices make loss ratio, claim frequency, severity, and premium share comparable without using unsupported bar layers. |
| Maximise portfolio profitability | Diagnose whether poor results come from frequency, severity, or both | KPI matrices and `stat_pointinterval()` | These methods show frequency, severity, and uncertainty while staying inside the approved ggplot technique set. |
| Retain low-risk profitable customers | Compare loyalty groups and identify profitable retained segments | `geom_tile()` + `geom_text()` KPI matrices for `loyalty_band` and bonus score | KPI matrices connect retention directly to loss ratio and premium share, showing whether loyal customers are profitable enough to protect. |
| Retain low-risk profitable customers | Avoid blunt rules that penalise good customers inside broad segments | `stat_halfeye()` + `geom_boxplot()` + pairwise Wilcoxon or `ggbetweenstats()` | Distribution-aware plots show overlap within groups, preventing overconfidence in stereotypes such as age, bonus score, or brand status. |
| Calibrate premium pricing | Detect hidden tail-risk patterns in short exposure or claimant groups | `geom_density_ridges_gradient()` with quantile shading | Ridgelines compare distribution shape across ordered groups and reveal whether a segment has a heavier adverse tail rather than just a higher mean. |
| Calibrate premium pricing | Identify interaction risk that univariate charts may hide | `geom_tile()` heatmaps with embedded labels | Heatmaps make two-way combinations, such as driver age by vehicle age, readable at a glance and useful for pricing segmentation. |
| Calibrate premium pricing | Assess dense numerical signals such as power-to-weight | `geom_hex()` + `geom_smooth(method = "gam")` | Hexbin plots avoid overplotting in large policy-level data, while the GAM smoother shows whether a practical non-linear pattern exists. |
| Reproducibility and communication | Test categorical myths with statistical context | `ggbarstats()` and `ggbetweenstats()` | These approved ggplot extensions combine visual comparison with statistical evidence for categorical and numeric segment differences. |

These choices also support the mythbusting structure. A myth is not confirmed by one chart alone; it is judged by the combined evidence of segment size, loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, and business relevance.

## 4.2 Feature Selection and Recoding

Only variables needed for the 10 research questions are retained. Raw code values are recoded into stakeholder-readable labels.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
premium_brands <- c(
  "AUDI", "BMW", "FERRARI", "HUMMER", "INFINITI", "JAGUAR",
  "LAND ROVER", "LEXUS", "MASERATI", "MERCEDES", "MINI",
  "PORSCHE", "SAAB", "VOLVO"
)

portfolio <- portfolio_raw |>
  select(
    insured_id, year,
    policy_type, policy_status, business_type, payment_frequency, bonus_score,
    driver_age, vehicle_age, fuel_type, vehicle_value, power_to_weight_ratio,
    vehicle_brand, municipality_type, circulation_area,
    total_premium, total_claims, total_incurred, total_exposure
  ) |>
  mutate(
    policy_type = recode(
      policy_type,
      "TP" = "Third party",
      "TPG" = "Third party + glass",
      "CC" = "Third party + add-ons",
      "COMP_E" = "Comprehensive with excess",
      "COMP_N" = "Comprehensive without excess"
    ),
    policy_type = factor(
      policy_type,
      levels = c(
        "Third party", "Third party + glass", "Third party + add-ons",
        "Comprehensive with excess", "Comprehensive without excess"
      )
    ),
    policy_status = recode(policy_status, "A" = "Active", "C" = "Cancelled"),
    business_type = recode(business_type, "NB" = "New business", "P" = "Portfolio"),
    payment_frequency = recode(
      payment_frequency,
      "A" = "Annual", "S" = "Semiannual", "Q" = "Quarterly"
    ),
    bonus_score = recode(bonus_score, "G" = "Good", "N" = "Neutral", "B" = "Bad"),
    bonus_score = factor(bonus_score, levels = c("Good", "Neutral", "Bad")),
    fuel_type = recode(fuel_type, "D" = "Diesel", "G" = "Gasoline", .missing = "Unknown"),
    municipality_type = recode(
      municipality_type,
      "I" = "Inland", "C" = "Coastal", "IS" = "Islands"
    ),
    circulation_area = recode(circulation_area, "U" = "Urban", "R" = "Rural"),
    vehicle_brand = replace_na(vehicle_brand, "Unknown"),
    brand_tier = if_else(vehicle_brand %in% premium_brands, "Premium brand", "Mainstream brand"),
    geo_segment = str_c(municipality_type, " - ", circulation_area),
    across(
      c(
        policy_status, business_type, payment_frequency, fuel_type,
        municipality_type, circulation_area, vehicle_brand, brand_tier, geo_segment
      ),
      as_factor
    )
  )
```

## 4.3 Derived Analytical Variables

Loss ratio is used as the main profitability metric. Claim frequency and claim severity are separated because the underwriting action differs when a segment is high-frequency versus high-severity.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
portfolio <- portfolio |>
  mutate(
    loss_ratio = safe_divide(total_incurred, total_premium),
    underwriting_result = total_premium - total_incurred,
    claim_flag = total_claims > 0,
    claim_frequency = safe_divide(total_claims, total_exposure),
    claim_severity = safe_divide(total_incurred, total_claims),
    profit_status = case_when(
      total_claims == 0 ~ "No claim",
      loss_ratio <= 1 ~ "Claim, still profitable",
      TRUE ~ "Loss-making"
    ),
    profit_status = factor(
      profit_status,
      levels = c("Loss-making", "Claim, still profitable", "No claim")
    ),
    exposure_band = cut(
      total_exposure,
      breaks = c(0, 0.35, 0.75, 0.95, Inf),
      labels = c("Very short (<0.35)", "Short (0.35-0.75)", "Medium (0.75-0.95)", "Full (>0.95)"),
      include.lowest = TRUE
    ),
    driver_age_band = cut(
      driver_age,
      breaks = c(17, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, Inf),
      labels = c("18-25", "26-35", "36-45", "46-55", "56-65", "66+"),
      right = TRUE
    ),
    vehicle_age_band = cut(
      vehicle_age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 3, 7, 12, 20, Inf),
      labels = c("0-3", "4-7", "8-12", "13-20", "21+"),
      right = TRUE
    ),
    vehicle_value_band = ntile(vehicle_value, 5),
    vehicle_value_band = factor(
      vehicle_value_band,
      labels = c("Lowest", "Low", "Middle", "High", "Highest")
    ),
    same_insured_years = ave(
      year,
      insured_id,
      FUN = function(x) length(unique(x))
    ),
    loyalty_band = case_when(
      same_insured_years >= 3 ~ "Observed all 3 years",
      same_insured_years == 2 ~ "Observed 2 years",
      TRUE ~ "Observed 1 year"
    ),
    loyalty_band = factor(
      loyalty_band,
      levels = c("Observed 1 year", "Observed 2 years", "Observed all 3 years")
    )
  )

loss_ratio_cap_99 <- quantile(
  portfolio$loss_ratio[is.finite(portfolio$loss_ratio)],
  probs = 0.99,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

portfolio <- portfolio |>
  mutate(loss_ratio_capped_99 = pmin(loss_ratio, loss_ratio_cap_99))
```
:::


## 4.4 Helper Summary Tables


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
segment_summary <- function(data, segment_var) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na({{ segment_var }})) |>
    group_by({{ segment_var }}) |>
    summarise(
      policies = n(),
      exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
      premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
      claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
      incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
      underwriting_result = sum(underwriting_result, na.rm = TRUE),
      loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
      claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
      claim_severity = incurred / claims,
      claim_rate = mean(claim_flag, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(premium))
}
```

# 5 Exploratory Data Analysis

## 5.1 Portfolio at a Glance

**Research questions supported:** RQ1 and RQ2.

**Technique justification:** A patchwork dashboard combines the year trend, loss ratio, claim frequency, and underwriting result in one view. This is more intuitive than separate charts because the reader can immediately see whether deterioration is caused by loss ratio movement, claim frequency movement, or exposure scale.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
year_long <- year_summary |>
  select(year, premium, incurred, underwriting_result, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, exposure) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(premium, incurred, underwriting_result, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, exposure),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      "premium" = "Premium",
      "incurred" = "Incurred loss",
      "underwriting_result" = "Underwriting result",
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim frequency",
      "exposure" = "Exposure"
    ),
```

## 8.4 Statistical Validation

**Technique justification:** Statistical tests are used as directional validation, not as a replacement for visual interpretation. With a large dataset, very small differences can become statistically significant, so practical significance still depends on visual effect size and premium exposure.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kw_test <- function(variable) {
  formula <- as.formula(str_c("loss_ratio_capped_99 ~ ", variable))
  kruskal.test(formula, data = portfolio) |>
    tidy() |>
    mutate(test = "Kruskal-Wallis", variable = variable)
}

chisq_test <- function(variable) {
  tbl <- table(portfolio[[variable]], portfolio$claim_flag)
  chisq.test(tbl) |>
    tidy() |>
    mutate(test = "Chi-square", variable = variable)
}

spearman_test <- function(variable) {
  cor.test(
    portfolio[[variable]],
    portfolio$loss_ratio_capped_99,
    method = "spearman",
    exact = FALSE
  ) |>
    tidy() |>
    mutate(test = "Spearman", variable = variable)
}

validation_tbl <- bind_rows(

    p_value = p.value
  ) |>
  arrange(p_value)
```
